headline: Connecticut ranks last among New England states in new energy-efficiency study
dek: WalletHub placed Connecticut 26th nationally and behind every other New England state in a ranking that combines household and vehicle energy-use measures.
body: Connecticut ranked last among the six New England states in WalletHub’s [2026 energy-efficiency study](https://wallethub.com/edu/most-and-least-energy-efficient-states/7354), a result that puts a fresh number on the region’s debate over utility costs, home heating and transportation. The study placed Connecticut 26th among the 48 states it evaluated, while Vermont ranked second nationally, Massachusetts fifth, Maine 12th, Rhode Island 14th and New Hampshire 22nd. Alaska and Hawaii were excluded because of data limitations, according to WalletHub.

The ranking is not a direct scorecard of Connecticut’s climate policy or a finding that every home in the state uses more energy than homes elsewhere. WalletHub combined two dimensions: home energy efficiency and auto energy efficiency. Its home measure compares residential energy consumption per person with annual heating and cooling degree days, an adjustment intended to account for different weather conditions. The auto measure incorporates vehicle-fuel efficiency and miles driven per person.

Connecticut’s overall score was 57.94. The state ranked 31st in home energy efficiency and 16th in auto energy efficiency. Those component rankings help explain why the overall result can look different from assessments focused on public programs or building policy: the WalletHub formula gives home and auto efficiency equal weight, while its underlying data also reflect how much people drive and how much energy homes consume relative to local weather.

The study was released Oct. 13 using data collected through Sept. 15 from the U.S. Census Bureau, the National Climatic Data Center, the U.S. Energy Information Administration and the Federal Highway Administration. WalletHub said the purpose was to compare how much energy states use in homes and vehicles, not to estimate an individual household’s bill or determine which state has the lowest utility prices.

That distinction matters for Connecticut residents heading into the heating season. [The Connecticut Post](https://www.ctpost.com/business/article/connecticut-energy-efficiency-wallethub-ranking-22475557.php), which reported on the ranking Oct. 14, noted that the U.S. Department of Energy estimates energy-efficiency measures can reduce household utility costs by as much as 25 percent. The savings available to a particular household will depend on the building, heating system, weather, driving patterns and the cost of the work, so the national ranking does not predict what any one resident will pay.

Energy experts quoted by the Connecticut Post pointed to relatively low-cost steps such as weather stripping, insulation, LED bulbs and low-flow shower heads. They also discussed heat pumps as a possible way to combine heating and cooling efficiency, depending on a home’s location and existing system. A home energy audit can help identify which improvements are likely to provide the best return rather than treating every upgrade as equally useful.

Connecticut already operates a statewide efficiency system through [Energize Connecticut](https://www.energizect.com/eeb-statewide-energy-efficiency-dashboard), an initiative involving the state, utilities and the Connecticut Green Bank. The program says its rebates, consultations and other services are funded through charges on electric and natural-gas bills and are guided by the Energy Efficiency Board and regulated by the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority. Its public dashboard tracks participation, spending and other program measures, giving residents a separate way to evaluate the state’s efficiency efforts.

The next question is how state programs and household decisions translate into future rankings and lower bills. WalletHub’s study does not identify a single cause for Connecticut’s position, and it does not measure every factor that shapes energy affordability, such as utility rate design, housing age or access to financing. What it does show is a regional contrast: Vermont and Massachusetts scored near the top nationally, while Connecticut’s combined home-and-auto result lagged the rest of New England.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Connecticut ranks last in New England energy efficiency study
seoDescription: A new WalletHub study ranks Connecticut 26th nationally and last in New England after comparing home and auto energy efficiency.
